# Does the endpoint occupy a sample?

[Predict the coordinates before you run the code.]{.lesson-deck}
:::

Before choosing a stencil or an FFT, decide what the endpoints mean. Five
samples on a periodic interval and five samples including both endpoints
are different grids, even when their physical bounds are identical.

## Count intervals before dividing

For $N$ periodic samples on $[a,b)$, there are $N$ intervals around the
periodic cycle: $h=(b-a)/N$. For $N$ samples including both ends of a closed
interval, there are $N-1$ intervals: $h=(b-a)/(N-1)$. OpenPFC's
`domain::from_bounds` makes this choice independently for each axis.

```{.cpp include="model.cpp" snippet="spacing" dedent=2}
```

With $N=5$ and $[a,b]=[0,2\pi]$, the periodic x coordinates stop at
$8\pi/5$. The closed-grid coordinates include $2\pi$. In both cases
`domain::upper` returns the requested bound. On the periodic grid that
bound is an image of the first sample, rather than a sixth stored sample.

## Make the convention explicit

```sh
openpfc run model.cpp input.json --launcher=none
```

This source-driven lesson ignores the empty input file; edit its constants
to experiment. Its CSV is printed to standard output. Change the sample
count in both the domain and loop, then predict the last coordinate.
Keep every nonperiodic axis at least two samples wide in this experiment.

Periodicity is geometric metadata here. It does not choose a derivative,
exchange a halo, or impose a boundary equation by itself. Compare the
[periodic heat stencil](../../heat/finite-differences/index.qmd) with
explicit boundary equations.
The regression checks all ten coordinates against independent interval
counts. The exact contract is in the public
[domain header](https://github.com/VTT-ProperTune/OpenPFC/blob/master/include/openpfc/kernel/data/domain.hpp).

The complete [C++ model](model.cpp) and [starting input](input.json)
are available with this lesson.
